title: FSST batched decode + substring prefilter bundle (q13)
summary:
Combined two changes for scans of FSST string columns. q13 measured -15.1%, -15.3% and -15.8% across three bench runs, with one outlier at -3.4%; all other templates were within noise.

1) src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp: a new FSSTScanState::DecompressStrings, used by both StringScanPartial (flat decode) and Select.
- It decodes each vector's strings back to back into shared heap allocations. Each allocation holds up to 64KB of worst-case output (8 bytes per compressed byte), plus 32 bytes of slack.
- Each string's write bound is the space left in the allocation, which always covers the worst case of the strings still to come.
- Strings that fit inline (12 bytes or less) are copied into their string_t, so their bytes are not kept in the heap. The allocation is shrunk to the bytes actually used.
- Decoding no longer goes through duckdb_fsst_decompress. It uses a simple loop that handles one code per iteration: copy the 8-byte symbol, add len[code], and copy the literal byte after an escape. This is safe because the symbol-table import always sets len to 1..8. An escape as the last byte throws a corrupt-file error.
- The all-values-inlined case keeps the old per-string path.

2) src/storage/table/column_segment.cpp: a substring prefilter for ExpressionFilter.
- It applies to LIKE (`~~`), NOT LIKE (`!~~`) and contains, optionally wrapped in NOT. The first argument must be the column itself (VARCHAR) and the second a non-NULL VARCHAR constant.
- The needle is the longest literal between '%'/'_' wildcards, or the whole contains argument, and must be at least 2 bytes.
- Strings stored back to back in memory are grouped into runs. Each run is searched once with an SSE2 first-byte/last-byte scan (overlapping final block, scalar fallback), and each hit is mapped to its row. Hits that cross a row boundary are rejected.
- Only rows that contain the needle are passed to the original expression. In the negated case, non-NULL rows without the needle pass directly. NULL rows always fail.
- A fresh SelectionVector is always built. Anything that does not match these conditions falls back to the existing path.

Measurements (CPU time from EXPLAIN ANALYZE; hot wall times from repeated runs):
- Scanning lineitem with `l_comment <> 'x'`: 6.88s → 4.06s CPU; hot wall time is about 278ms now (no hot timing of the old build).
- The orders NOT LIKE scan costs 2.12s CPU against 1.98s for a trivial `<>` filter on the same column, so the LIKE evaluation itself is now nearly free.
- Full bench runs: the geomean came out -1.7% and +1.0%. Templates that looked slower once (q08 +7.5%, q16 +9.7%, q22 +6.7%) came back to noise when rerun (q08 -3.6%, q16 +1.2%).
- The bench showed results correct on every visible template.
- Extra checks:
  - sum(hash(col)) on l_comment, o_comment and p_name was identical between the new decode path and the original one (reached with enable_fsst_vectors=true).
  - NOT LIKE, LIKE, NOT contains, contains and a LIKE pattern with '_' gave the same counts as the same filter on `col||''` (which is not pushed into the scan), on both the orders data and a temp table with NULLs, inlined strings and needles split across rows.
notes:
- The key finding: FSST scan cost was about 100ns per string almost regardless of length (27-byte strings 115ns/row, 48-byte strings 133ns/row), so it is per-string overhead, not per-byte work. The 4-code fast loop and tail branches of duckdb_fsst_decompress cost more than the decode itself.
- Follow-up idea: apply the same simple decode loop to FSSTVector::DecompressVector (src/common/types/vector.cpp) and to dict_fsst decompression. Both still call duckdb_fsst_decompress per string.
- Bench noise on this machine is about ±8% per template in a single run. Rerun before trusting a regression.
- The q13 scan now spends about 1.9s CPU on decode-plus-scan and almost nothing on the LIKE itself. The next q13 target is the perfect hash group-by (about 1.0s CPU) or skipping decode entirely, e.g. by searching compressed codes.
